lines: The bike chain wants to go public and raise one hundred million dollars. Follow that money and you meet almost every job on Wall Street.
Every job sits on one of two sides. The sell side sells deals and services, mainly investment banks. The buy side invests money: funds of every kind.

An investment bank advises on mergers, underwrites new stocks and bonds, trades for clients, and writes research. On a mid-size IPO, banks take about seven percent: seven million of the chain's hundred million.
A commercial bank is different: it takes deposits and makes loans. On the buy side are asset managers, pension funds, hedge funds, private equity and wealth managers.

Each gets paid its own way. A wealth manager charging one percent on five hundred thousand dollars earns five thousand a year. A hedge fund charging two and twenty on a hundred million that earns ten percent takes four million, leaving investors six percent.
Inside each firm, the front office brings in money, the middle office manages risk and compliance, and the back office settles trades.

At a bank, most people start as analysts right out of college, then climb to associate, vice president, director and managing director. Most analyst jobs go to students who interned the summer before.
